requirements.title: Govern: a culture and structures for AI risk management
Risk policies, processes and practices are in place and effective
AI legal and regulatory requirements understood and documented
Trustworthy AI characteristics built into policies and practices
Level of risk management activity set from risk tolerance
Risk management process set by transparent policies and controls
Monitoring and periodic review of the risk process planned
Inventory of AI systems, resourced by risk priority
Safe decommissioning and phase-out of AI systems
Accountability structures for AI risk management
Roles, responsibilities and communication lines documented
AI risk management training for personnel and partners
Executive leadership responsible for AI risk decisions
Diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility in AI risk work
AI risk decisions informed by a diverse team
Roles for human-AI configurations and oversight defined
A culture that considers and communicates AI risk
Critical-thinking and safety-first mindset fostered
Teams document AI risks and impacts and communicate them
Practices enable AI testing, incident identification and sharing
Engagement with relevant AI actors
External feedback on individual and societal impacts integrated
Adjudicated feedback from AI actors fed into design
Third-party software, data and supply-chain risks
Policies for third-party AI risks, including IP infringement
Contingency for failures of high-risk third-party data or AI
Map: context and risks of the AI system
Context established and understood
Intended purposes, context, laws and deployment settings documented
Interdisciplinary and diverse actors establish the context
Organisational mission and AI goals documented
Business value or context of use defined or re-evaluated
Organisational risk tolerances determined and documented
System requirements elicited; socio-technical design choices
Categorisation of the AI system
Tasks and methods of the AI system defined
Knowledge limits and human use and oversight of outputs documented
Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations documented
Capabilities, usage, benefits and costs against benchmarks
Potential benefits examined and documented
Potential costs of AI errors examined and documented
Targeted application scope specified and documented
Operator and practitioner proficiency processes defined
Human oversight processes defined, assessed and documented
Risks and benefits mapped for all components, third-party included
Technology and legal risks of components mapped, IP included
Internal risk controls for components identified and documented
Impacts on individuals, groups, organisations and society
Likelihood and magnitude of each identified impact documented
Regular engagement and feedback on impacts in place
Measure: analysing, assessing and tracking AI risks
Appropriate methods and metrics identified and applied
Metrics for the most significant mapped risks selected
Metrics and control effectiveness regularly reassessed
Independent or non-developer experts involved in assessments
AI systems evaluated for trustworthy characteristics
Test sets, metrics and TEVV tools documented
Human-subject evaluations protected and representative
Performance measured in conditions like deployment
Functionality and behaviour monitored in production
Validity and reliability shown; generalisation limits documented
Safety risks evaluated; system shown to fail safely
Security and resilience evaluated and documented
Transparency and accountability risks examined
Model explained and validated; outputs interpreted in context
Privacy risk examined and documented
Fairness and bias evaluated and documented
Environmental impact and sustainability assessed
Effectiveness of TEVV metrics and processes evaluated
Tracking of identified AI risks over time
Existing, unanticipated and emergent risks tracked regularly
Risk tracking where measurement is not yet possible
Channels to report problems and appeal outcomes
Feedback on the efficacy of measurement
Measurement tied to deployment context and expert input
Trustworthiness results validated with experts and AI actors
Performance changes from consultation and field data documented
Manage: prioritising and treating AI risks
Mapped and measured risks prioritised, responded to and managed
Decision whether the system meets its purpose and should proceed
Risk treatment prioritised by impact, likelihood and resources
Responses to high-priority risks planned and documented
Negative residual risks documented for acquirers and end users
Strategies to maximise benefits and minimise negative impacts
Resources and non-AI alternatives considered
Mechanisms sustain the value of deployed systems
Response to and recovery from previously unknown risks
Means to supersede, disengage or deactivate a deviating system
Third-party AI risks and benefits managed
Third-party risks monitored and controls documented
Pre-trained models monitored in regular maintenance
Risk treatments and communication plans documented and monitored
Post-deployment monitoring plans implemented
Continual improvement built into system updates
Incidents and errors communicated, tracked and recovered from

notes: The AI RMF is voluntary. Its subcategories are outcomes, not obligations; a covered cell means that reviewed audit work bears on the outcome, never that an organisation conforms to the framework. Every category lists all its subcategories and every function all its categories, so the groups are exhaustive.
